16-2.title: India has no national outpatient chronic-disease certificate; use ESIC, CGHS, PM-JAY or your state scheme
16-2.inPlainWords: India does not run a national outpatient certification that unlocks reimbursement across states. The cover depends on the scheme: ESIC for insured workers, CGHS for central government staff, PM-JAY for eligible households, and a state health scheme. For a chronic disease, ask the scheme's empanelled hospital what is covered, and keep the prescriptions and bills. eSanjeevani offers a free online consultation in many states.
16-2.benefit: PM-JAY covers hospitalisation for eligible households and has a list of packages; some states add outpatient cover. ESIC provides sickness and medical benefit to insured persons and dependants. CGHS covers central government employees and pensioners at wellness centres and empanelled hospitals. eSanjeevani, run by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, provides teleconsultation. A referral is usually needed for a specialist or a higher facility.
16-2.cost: PM-JAY is free for eligible households; ESIC and CGHS are contribution or subscription based. A private policy is separate.
16-2.caveats: A 'chronic disease card' sold by an agent is not a government scheme. The package list and the empanelled hospital change. A pre-authorisation may be needed for a planned admission.
16-2.sources: National Health Authority, PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Central Government Health Scheme. <https://cghs.gov.in/>; eSanjeevani. <https://esanjeevani.mohfw.gov.in/>

16-3.cost: A checkup at a government hospital or a health and wellness centre is free or carries only a nominal registration fee; a private clinic or laboratory charges separately. A trip to the hospital and the wait for results also take time. The main difficulty is that you must go regularly, which can easily be put off.
16-3.caveats: Be sure to record at least four items each time: the date, the measurement value, the medication being used, and its dosage. Taking a photo of the lab report with your phone works just as well. The key is to keep everything in the same place rather than scattering it across multiple notes. If keeping to the routine becomes difficult, or you feel low, Tele-MANAS on 14416 gives free telephone support in Indian languages.
16-3.sources: author’s experience, no direct literature; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Indian Council of Medical Research. <https://www.icmr.gov.in/>; Tele-MANAS. <https://telemanas.mohfw.gov.in/>

16-4.caveats: Always consult your doctor before trying any supplements. Certain supplements may interact with prescription medications, affecting concentrations of anticoagulants and anti-rejection drugs in the bloodstream. In India, medicines are approved and licensed by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, so a product sold as a cure without a drug licence is not a medicine.
16-4.sources: Author’s experience, no direct literature; see Section 6 for relevant evidence; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Indian Council of Medical Research. <https://www.icmr.gov.in/>; Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. <https://cdsco.gov.in/>

16-5.title: Ask whether your clinic will give a longer repeat prescription for a stable chronic condition
16-5.cost: Nothing to ask. The medicine itself is charged at the scheme or facility rate.
16-5.inPlainWords: India has no all-India rule that fixes how many weeks of medicine a clinic may hand out at one visit. What you get depends on the facility, the state drug policy and your scheme: ESIC, CGHS, PM-JAY or a state health scheme. If the condition is stable and the prescription has not changed, ask the doctor for a longer repeat supply so that you do not have to travel every month. A government hospital or a health and wellness centre (Ayushman Arogya Mandir) can renew a prescription for a stable condition, and eSanjeevani gives a free teleconsultation in many states.
16-5.benefit: For a stable chronic condition the monthly trip is often the largest cost, not the medicine. A longer repeat supply, a teleconsultation or a nearby health and wellness centre removes most of that. Under CGHS and ESIC the follow-up and the medicine run through the wellness centre or the empanelled dispensary, so ask there before travelling to a hospital. A generic medicine from a Jan Aushadhi Kendra usually costs less than the branded equivalent.
16-5.caveats: The doctor decides whether a longer supply is safe. It is for a confirmed diagnosis with an unchanged regimen, not for a new symptom. Some medicines, including controlled drugs and drugs that need monitoring, are limited to a shorter supply. If the clinic does not stock the medicine, ask for the nearest Jan Aushadhi Kendra or the scheme's empanelled pharmacy. PM-JAY covers hospitalisation, not routine outpatient medicine, so check the outpatient rule of your own scheme instead of assuming cover.
16-5.sources: Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Central Government Health Scheme. <https://cghs.gov.in/>; National Health Authority, PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; eSanjeevani. <https://esanjeevani.mohfw.gov.in/>; Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Bureau of India, Jan Aushadhi. <https://janaushadhi.gov.in/>

16-6.title: Before you register with a family doctor, ask what the clinic covers and whether it is free under a scheme
16-6.inPlainWords: India does not have a single family-doctor registration scheme. The nearest public route is the Ayushman Arogya Mandir (health and wellness centre), where an ANM or a community health officer provides primary care, and the ASHA worker links the household to the system. A private family physician is paid per visit or by an annual retainer. Ask which services are free, which are charged, and where you are referred.
16-6.benefit: The National Health Mission runs Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (formerly health and wellness centres) with a defined package of primary-care services. The National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) supports screening for hypertension, diabetes and common cancers at these centres. PM-JAY covers hospitalisation for eligible households, and eSanjeevani provides teleconsultation. A private clinic's annual retainer is a contract; read what it excludes. The Clinical Establishments Act and the state rules apply to a private clinic.
16-6.cost: A public health and wellness centre is free. A private retainer or a per-visit fee varies.
16-6.caveats: A 'family doctor' plan may exclude specialist care and diagnostics. Check the doctor's registration with the state medical council. A public centre may not have a doctor every day.
16-6.sources: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Health Mission. <https://nhm.gov.in/>; National Health Authority. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>

16-7.cost: At a government hospital or a health and wellness centre a dilated eye exam carries only the usual outpatient charge, while a private clinic or an optician bills separately. Foot exams are usually part of a routine outpatient visit, so they add no separate charge. The real challenge is remembering to get these checks done when neither your eyes nor your feet feel any discomfort.

16-8.caveats: This measure reduces recurrence rates by roughly 55% at zero cost, making it the most cost-effective recommendation in this section according to our ranking criteria. The key metric to monitor is 24-hour urine volume, which should reach at least 2–2.5 liters — not simply the amount of water you drink. People who sweat heavily or work in hot environments need to drink even more. This trial involved only patients experiencing their first idiopathic calcium stone episode; different types of stones — such as uric acid, infection-related, or cystine stones — require different treatment approaches. Anyone with a history of kidney stones should undergo a stone composition analysis and a 24-hour urine test to determine whether medication is needed. Do not cut calcium intake to prevent stones; see section 6, item 21 for more details. Severe flank or abdominal pain during a stone episode requires immediate medical attention — drinking more water alone will not resolve it. Non-painful blood in the urine may indicate other conditions; see section 1, item 27 for further information.

16-9.title: Long‑term use of uric‑acid‑lowering drugs after a gout diagnosis to keep levels below 360 µmol/L
16-9.cost: Allopurinol is an inexpensive medicine, but the price depends on the brand, the strength and the pharmacy, so check it at a Jan Aushadhi Kendra or a licensed pharmacy. At first, blood uric‑acid levels must be checked every few weeks to adjust the dose; once stable, checks can be done every few months. For the first 3–6 months, a second medication to prevent flare‑ups is also required. The difficulty is that patients must keep taking it even when they feel no pain.
16-9.inPlainWords: Gout requires lifelong use of uric‑acid‑lowering drugs to keep levels under 360 µmol/L; painkillers alone are insufficient. In a study where nurses helped patients adjust their dose based on lab results, 95 % reached the target after two years, compared with only 30 % of patients seen by regular doctors. Even after reaching the target, medication must not be stopped. Diet changes alone cannot bring levels down to this point, and abstaining from alcohol lowers them by just 1.6 mg/dL.
16-9.benefit: In a randomized controlled trial of 517 adults who had experienced gout attacks within the previous 12 months, one group received nurse‑led education and dose adjustments to achieve the target level, while the other continued routine care. After two years, 95 % of the intervention group versus 30 % of the control group had uric‑acid levels below 360 µmol/L (6 mg/dL). The odds of success were 3.18 times higher in the intervention group (RR 3.18, 95 % CI 2.42–4.18; P < 0.0001). Secondary outcomes — attack frequency, tophus formation, and quality of life — also improved. Each additional quality‑adjusted life year gained cost £5,066. Follow‑up data showed that 82 % of participants reported zero attacks in the previous year, versus a median of one attack for the control group (P < 0.001). The proportion still on therapy was 1.19 times higher in the intervention group (adjusted RR 1.19, 1.09–1.30). The 2020 American College of Rheumatology guidelines recommend uric‑acid‑lowering therapy for patients with tophi, bone erosion on imaging, or ≥2 attacks per year; the target is <6 mg/dL, achieved by regular monitoring and dose titration, with allopurinol as first‑line therapy, especially for those with stage 3 or higher chronic kidney disease. Anti‑inflammatory prophylaxis is advised for 3–6 months at initiation. Observational data indicate that after successful control, many patients can discontinue medication without relapse; however, only 13 % remained flare‑free over five years. Alcohol restriction lowers uric‑acid levels by 1.6 mg/dL, while a single beer raises them by 0.16 mg/dL; healthier diets have far smaller effects. Debate persists over optimal drug choice: allopurinol is favored for its efficacy, safety, and low cost, though patients with cardiovascular disease or recent events may be switched to other agents per FDA warnings. The CARES trial linked febuxostat to a 22% higher risk of all‑cause mortality (HR 1.22) and a 34% higher risk of cardiovascular death (HR 1.34) versus allopurinol; the European FAST trial found no such increase. Urine alkalinization is not recommended for uricosuric agents due to lack of evidence. Adequate hydration is essential, especially for patients with kidney stones or advanced CKD.
16-9.caveats: Controversy exists: different countries recommend different first‑line drugs. The U.S. guideline favors allopurinol and advises avoiding febuxostat in patients with cardiovascular disease, whereas the FAST trial found no increased risk with febuxostat. Allopurinol can cause severe cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions, and the 2020 ACR guideline recommends testing for the HLA‑B*5801 allele before starting it in people from populations where that allele is common — people of Han, Korean and Thai descent and African‑American patients; there is no national requirement in India to test before prescribing, so ask your doctor whether testing is worth doing for you. Initiation of therapy can temporarily increase flare‑ups, so anti‑inflammatory prophylaxis for 3–6 months is mandatory; discontinuing uric‑acid‑lowering drugs because of pain is a common cause of treatment failure. When an attack occurs, additional anti‑inflammatory medication should be added per medical advice, not the uric‑acid‑lowering drug. Asymptomatic hyperuricemia is addressed separately in Section 6, Item 19. Sugar‑sweetened beverages and alcohol are discussed in Section 2, Items 7 and 19.
